newsitem.title: USA: Pork prices add gains on Taiwan news, grains fall.
newsitem.headline: Pork prices add gains on Taiwan news, grains fall.

text.p: Pork futures soared the daily trading limit for a second straight day on Friday on furious buying from speculators and commercial firms who believe pork exports will jump due to Taiwan's exit from the world market.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, May pork belly futures closed up the 3-cent a pound daily limit at 79.300 cents and June lean hogs up the 2-cent a pound limit at 80.150 cents.

The Taiwan Council of Agriculture announced Thursday it was banning all exports of fresh and frozen pork temporarily due to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, a contagious disease that may worsen due to shortages of vaccines.
Exports may not resume for months, traders said.

"It would seem there would be some commercial opportunities for our pork exports into traditional Taiwan pork markets," Chris Goldthwait, general sales manager for the U.S. Agriculture Department, told Reuters.

Pork is one of Taiwan's biggest export items. Taiwan provides 45 percent of Japan's pork imports, while the U.S. has only 23 percent of that market. Taiwan has been shipping 16,000 metric tons of pork a month to Japan.
IBP Inc., a leading exporter of meat products, said Japanese buyers had already made inquiries about acquiring additional supplies of pork.
"We have seen increased interest in our product from Japanese customers," IBP spokesman Gary Mickelsen said. "But what it will mean long-term will be difficult to say."
Glenn Grimes, an agricultural economist at the University of Missouri, said the United States was likely to gain up to two-thirds of Taiwan's share of pork exports to Japan.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, grain prices closed lower as speculation grew that Taiwan would sharply cut back on feed imports as it culls its diseased swine herd.
May corn closed down 4-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.00-1/4.

Taiwan was the number three foreign buyer of U.S. corn and soybeans last year. But on Friday, Taiwan's Members Feed Industry Group passed on a tender to buy two shipments of U.S. or Argentine corn and Taiwanese buyers also declined to purchase soybeans.

"The trade realized this Taiwan foot-and-mouth disease was probably a bigger issue than was believed yesterday," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities. "When we saw tenders passed overnight, that was the wakeup call."

A survey of five Taiwan grain importers found that all expected significant reductions in corn imports, with most estimating the downturn at about 1.2 million tons or nearly 20 percent of the island's annual imports of 6.5 million tons.
May soybeans fell 9-1/2 cents a bushel to $8.42-1/2.
Wheat prices also fell on worries about U.S. prices being too high for foreign buyers. May wheat closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $3.90.

Algeria passed on a tender to buy 75,000 tons of milling wheat on Friday. But after the close of futures trading, Egypt announced a snap tender to buy 150,000 tons of U.S. or Australian wheat to take advantage of the price drop.
Gold prices in New York remained firm ahead of next week's Federal Reserve Board meeting. April gold at the COMEX in New York closed up $1.30 an ounce at $353.50.

"In the next couple of days, gold prices are expected to remain in the same general area in anticipation of next Tuesday's FOMC meeting in which the Federal Reserve will decide whether or not to raise interest rates," said CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil futures closed lower on weak physical demand and ample supplies.
May crude oil fell 34 cents a barrel to close at $21.51.
"With the April contract off the board, the short covering is over and the market is refocusing on the weak fundamentals of the cash market," said trader Nauman Barakat at Prudential Securities.
April heating oil closed up 0.04 cent at 55.98 cents a gallon and April gasoline up 0.06 cent a gallon at 67.64 cents.
